entities.name: Frederick de la Roche
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Frederick de la Roche (died October 30, 1174) emerged as a central figure in the Latin East, serving as the sixth Latin Archbishop of Tyre from 1164 until his death. His significance stems from his dual capacity as a powerful ecclesiastical prelate and the chief diplomat and chancellor for King Amalric I of Jerusalem, navigating the intricate political and religious currents of the Crusader states during a critical period of external threats and internal consolidation. Hailing from Lorraine, he was a member of the influential family of the counts of La Roche, which provided him with crucial connections to European nobility and papal authority.

As Archbishop of Tyre, Frederick presided over one of the most strategically vital sees in the Kingdom of Jerusalem, a city renowned for its maritime and commercial importance. His tenure as chancellor under King Amalric I (reigned 1163–1174) positioned him at the epicenter of royal administration, where he was instrumental in formulating the kingdom's foreign policy. A crowning achievement was his extensive diplomatic mission to Europe from 1169 to 1171, during which he tirelessly sought military and financial aid for the beleaguered Crusader states, engaging powerful monarchs like Louis VII of France and Emperor Frederick I Barbarossa, following Amalric's costly failed invasion of Egypt. He also played a key role in negotiating the politically significant marriage between Amalric I and Maria Comnena, niece of Byzantine Emperor Manuel I Comnenus, which temporarily solidified the alliance with the Byzantine Empire.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Frederick de la Roche was a pivotal figure in the diplomatic and ecclesiastical landscape of the Latin East, effectively serving as the chief diplomat for the Kingdom of Jerusalem during a crucial decade. His efforts to secure Western aid and forge alliances significantly shaped the kingdom's foreign policy and provided vital intelligence to Europe.
